tip: The inseparable prefix 'be-' gives no 'ge-' in the participle: 'begeistert', not 'gebegeistert'.
Adding '-in' makes the female form: 'der Weber' becomes 'die Weberin' (female weaver).
Separable verbs slot 'ge-' inside for the participle: 'durchgeprobt', from 'durch' and 'geprobt'.
With two objects, the dative person normally comes before the accusative thing: 'dem Kind ein Geschenk'.
The feminine dative takes '-er' on the possessive: 'seiner Mutter' (to his mother).
With a dative person 'leihen' means lend to, without one it means borrow: 'leiht seinem Freund das Auto'.
A dative object can mean for someone: 'kaufe meinem Sohn ein Spielzeug' (buy my son a toy).
'Patient' is a weak noun, adding '-en' in the dative: 'dem Patienten' (to the patient).
The recipient takes the dative pronoun 'dir', not 'dich': 'ich bringe dir' means I bring to you, while 'dich' would be the accusative object.
Before an uncountable noun 'viel' usually stays unchanged: 'viel Glück' (lots of luck).
Animals get 'Fressen', people get 'Essen': 'sein Fressen' is the dog's food.
The phrase 'jemandem eine Freude machen' means to make someone happy: 'ihren Freunden eine Freude'.
The verb 'schenken' means to give as a gift, unlike plain 'geben': 'schenkt seiner Mutter eine Kette'.
The verb 'teilnehmen' splits, 'teil' goes to the clause end: 'nimmt ... teil'.
The verb 'nachdenken' pairs with 'über' for the topic: 'denken ... über das Angebot nach' (think about).
The verb 'ablehnen' splits, 'ab' moves to the clause end: 'lehnen ... ab' (decline).
The verb 'einnicken' takes 'sein' in the Perfekt, it is a change of state: 'bin ... eingenickt' (dozed off).
Sports with 'spielen' normally drop the article: 'Fußball gespielt', not 'den Fußball'.
The verb 'vorlesen' splits and means read aloud to someone: 'liest ihren Kindern ... vor'.
Some regions carry an article, so you say 'in der': 'in der Toskana' (in Tuscany).
Masculine and neuter nouns often add '-es' in the genitive: 'seines Sohnes' (his son's).
The reflexive phrase 'sich etwas zuziehen' means to catch an illness: 'hat sich ... zugezogen'.
German fuses nouns into one, often with a link '-n': 'Tulpen' plus 'Zwiebeln' makes 'Tulpenzwiebeln'.
Verbs ending in '-ieren' form the participle without 'ge-': 'dokumentiert' (documented).
Before a noun, 'während' means during and takes the genitive: 'während der Vorlesung' (during the lecture).
The verb 'danken' takes dative for the person and 'für' for the reason: 'danke meiner Kollegin für den Rat'.
The verb 'drohen' takes a dative object: 'droht dem Einbrecher' (threatens the burglar).
Verbs with an inseparable prefix skip the usual 'ge-' in the participle: 'haben uns entschlossen' (decided), never 'geentschlossen'.
German parks the participle at the clause end: 'hat seine Meinung über das Thema geändert'. English keeps changed right after has, but German waits.
Movement verbs like 'kommen' take 'sein' in the Perfekt: 'bin ... gekommen'.
